name: Bohtan Neo-Aramaic
catalog_citation: Fox, Samuel Ethan. 2007. The Story of Mem u Zine in the Neo-Aramaic Dialect of Bohtan. In Cynthia L. Miller (ed.), Studies in Semitic and Afroasiatic Linguistics Presented to Gene B. Gragg (SAOC 60), 69-80. Chicago: Oriental Institute. Open PDF: https://isac.…
catalog_quote: There is a strong penultimate stress,3 and stress moves when a suffix is added: arxe ‘mill’ arxota ‘mills’ kebœn ‘I (masculine) want’ kebœnna ‘I (masculine) want her’ abra ‘son’ abreni ‘our son’ In most dialects, adding a clitic to a word generally does not cause stress to shift, as in this Jilu example: múdi ‘what’ múdi-la ‘what is it (feminine)?’ However, in Bohtan, even when clitics are added the stress usually shifts: brota ‘daughter, girl’ brotá-se ‘also the girl’ bata ‘house’ batá-la ‘she is (in) the house’ In the verb paradigm, stress sometimes deviates from the usual strong penultimate pattern. ... [fn. 3:] Because the great majority of words have penultimate stress, stress is not marked unless it is not penultimate.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote confirmed verbatim in the held open publisher PDF/text of Fox 2007 at p. 70 + fn. 3. (2) The deciding source is a first-hand sketch by the dialect's sole documenter, publisher-text grade, 2007; the classification (penultimate word stress, stress shifting with suffixes and usually with enclitics, listed verb-paradigm exceptions) is exactly what the passage says. (3) It is not the best available description: Fox's 2009 Gorgias reference grammar (175 pp, Glottolog 'grammar') exists and is not held; it is paywalled (DOI 10.31826/9781463217327) and only shadow-library copies appear online, so nothing was fetched sources. No instrumental or dedicated prosody study of Bohtan was found.
